scenes.visual: Title card 'Two Ledgers, One Kill' over a cartoon fox-like predator (ORANGE) and a hare-like prey (TEAL) facing each other. COLOUR MAP, same in both films: TEAL (#0e7c86) = prey; ORANGE (#e57200) = predators; dark ink = the orbit and labels; grey neutrals for other species. Symbols on screen exactly as in the lesson: N (prey), P (predators), N*, P*, r, a, e, m. Cream background, 16:9. Every number appears only as on-screen text. Animals and ledgers are simple cartoons labelled 'schematic'; phase-plane orbits and time series are computed from the Lotka-Volterra model with the lesson's worked numbers (r = 1, a = 0.01, e = 0.1, m = 0.5) and labelled 'computed'.

scenes.tts: If predators eat prey, why do predator numbers keep climbing after the prey have started to fall? The answer is in how one kill is counted.
scenes.visual: Two computed time-series curves draw left to right: TEAL prey curve rises and peaks; the ORANGE predator curve is still climbing after the TEAL curve has turned down. A question mark hovers over the gap between the two peaks. Axis labels 'time' and 'numbers'. Label 'computed'.
scenes.narration: If predators eat prey, why do predator numbers keep climbing after the prey have started to fall? The answer is in how one kill is counted.

scenes.tts: Every population keeps a ledger of births and deaths. Births push its numbers up, and deaths pull them down. Here are two ledgers, one for prey and one for predators.
scenes.visual: Two ledger books open side by side, TEAL 'prey ledger' and ORANGE 'predator ledger', each with a 'births' column (plus signs) and a 'deaths' column (minus signs). Entries tick in as the narrator speaks; a small population bar beside each ledger rises with births and falls with deaths. Label 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Every population keeps a ledger of births and deaths. Births push its numbers up, and deaths pull them down. Here are two ledgers, one for prey and one for predators.

scenes.tts: Now watch the kills. Each is a death in the prey's ledger. Each is also food, and on average, predators turn that food into births. So every kill is entered twice.
scenes.visual: An ORANGE predator catches TEAL prey, one after another. For each kill an arrow lifts a TEAL minus entry into the prey ledger's deaths column and drops a small food token into a TEAL-to-ORANGE 'food' tray. As tokens pile up, ORANGE plus entries appear in the predator ledger's births column, tagged 'e: average new predators per prey eaten (a rate, not one kill per birth)'. The words 'entered twice' stamp across both ledgers.
scenes.narration: Now watch the kills. Each is a death in the prey's ledger. Each is also food, and on average, predators turn that food into births. So every kill is entered twice.

scenes.tts: That double entry ties the two ledgers together. The more predators there are, the faster each prey dies. The more prey there are, the faster predators breed.
scenes.visual: A chain links the two ledgers. Left: a slider for predator numbers P; as it rises, the TEAL deaths column fills faster. Right: a slider for prey numbers N; as it rises, the ORANGE births column fills faster. On screen: 'per prey: r - aP', 'per predator: eaN - m'.
scenes.narration: That double entry ties the two ledgers together. The more predators there are, the faster each prey dies. The more prey there are, the faster predators breed.

scenes.tts: First ask when the prey stop changing. Each prey's birth rate stays fixed, but its risk of death grows with every predator. At one predator number, P star, the two balance.
scenes.caption: First ask when the prey stop changing. Each prey's birth rate stays fixed, but its risk of death grows with every predator. At one predator number, P*, the two balance.
scenes.visual: A vertical axis 'predators, P'. A TEAL balance scale: the 'births' pan holds steady while weights labelled 'risk' pile onto the 'deaths' pan as an ORANGE marker climbs the axis. At the level point a horizontal TEAL dashed line appears, labelled 'P* = r/a: prey stop changing'. Small TEAL arrows below the line point 'prey increase', above it 'prey decrease'.
scenes.narration: First ask when the prey stop changing. Each prey's birth rate stays fixed, but its risk of death grows with every predator. At one predator number, P*, the two balance.

scenes.tts: Now ask when the predators stop changing. Each predator must eat enough prey to replace itself. That happens at one prey number, N star. With more prey, predators increase. With fewer, they decrease.
scenes.caption: Now ask when the predators stop changing. Each predator must eat enough prey to replace itself. That happens at one prey number, N*. With more prey, predators increase. With fewer, they decrease.
scenes.visual: A horizontal axis 'prey, N'. An ORANGE predator icon with a stomach gauge; as a TEAL marker slides right along the axis the gauge fills; where it reads 'replaces itself' a vertical ORANGE dashed line drops, labelled 'N* = m/(ea): predators stop changing'. ORANGE arrows: right of the line 'predators increase', left 'predators decrease'.
scenes.narration: Now ask when the predators stop changing. Each predator must eat enough prey to replace itself. That happens at one prey number, N*. With more prey, predators increase. With fewer, they decrease.

scenes.tts: Put both thresholds on one picture, with prey across and predators up. The two lines cut it into four zones. Each zone has its own pair of directions.
scenes.visual: The two axes join into a phase plane: N across, P up. The TEAL horizontal line at P* and ORANGE vertical line at N* cross at a diamond labelled 'equilibrium (N*, P*)'. Four zones appear one at a time, each with a small grey arrow combining the TEAL and ORANGE directions: bottom right up-right, top right up-left, top left down-left, bottom left down-right.
scenes.narration: Put both thresholds on one picture, with prey across and predators up. The two lines cut it into four zones. Each zone has its own pair of directions.

scenes.tts: Start a dot in the bottom right, with many prey and few predators. Following the arrows, it circles the crossing point counter-clockwise, and returns to where it began.
scenes.visual: A dark dot starts in the bottom-right zone and moves counter-clockwise along a computed closed orbit around the diamond, leaving a dark ink trail. Below the plane, a time-series strip draws the TEAL prey curve and ORANGE predator curve in step with the dot. Label 'computed'.
scenes.narration: Start a dot in the bottom right, with many prey and few predators. Following the arrows, it circles the crossing point counter-clockwise, and returns to where it began.

scenes.tts: Stop the dot where the prey curve reaches its top. The prey have just peaked. Are the predators rising or falling?
scenes.visual: The dot freezes where the orbit crosses the TEAL P* line in the upper right. In the strip below, a marker sits on the TEAL peak; the ORANGE curve beside it is cut off at that moment. Two tags: 'rising?' and 'falling?'.
scenes.narration: Stop the dot where the prey curve reaches its top. The prey have just peaked. Are the predators rising or falling?

scenes.visual: Hold the frame; a 5-second countdown; caption 'Predict: prey just peaked. Predators rising or falling?'.

scenes.tts: Still rising. The prey are falling, but there are still more of them than N star. So each predator still eats more than it needs to replace itself.
scenes.caption: Still rising. The prey are falling, but there are still more of them than N*. So each predator still eats more than it needs to replace itself.
scenes.visual: The 'rising' tag lights. The frozen dot is shown well to the right of the ORANGE N* line; a bracket between the dot and the line is labelled 'prey still above N*'. The ORANGE curve in the strip resumes climbing.
scenes.narration: Still rising. The prey are falling, but there are still more of them than N*. So each predator still eats more than it needs to replace itself.

scenes.tts: The predators peak only when the prey drop through N star. So the predator peak comes after the prey peak. Nothing in the model builds in a delay. The lag comes from the bookkeeping.
scenes.caption: The predators peak only when the prey drop through N*. So the predator peak comes after the prey peak. Nothing in the model builds in a delay. The lag comes from the bookkeeping.
scenes.visual: The dot moves on and crosses the ORANGE N* line; the ORANGE curve in the strip peaks at that instant. A bracket between the TEAL peak and the ORANGE peak is labelled 'lag (computed)'. A crossed-out clock icon labelled 'no built-in delay'.
scenes.narration: The predators peak only when the prey drop through N*. So the predator peak comes after the prey peak. Nothing in the model builds in a delay. The lag comes from the bookkeeping.

scenes.tts: Start the dot somewhere else, and it traces a different loop. In this classical model, each start with both populations present and away from the crossing point keeps its own loop. Where it starts sets the size of the cycle.
scenes.visual: Two more dots start at different points and trace a smaller and a larger computed closed loop around the same diamond, nested inside each other; the diamond itself stays fixed. Label 'classical Lotka-Volterra model: each start with both populations present and away from the equilibrium keeps its own loop (computed)'.
scenes.narration: Start the dot somewhere else, and it traces a different loop. In this classical model, each start with both populations present and away from the crossing point keeps its own loop. Where it starts sets the size of the cycle.

scenes.tts: So every kill, entered in both ledgers, ties them together. In this simple model, each population's per capita growth rate is set by the other's numbers.
scenes.visual: Zoom out: the two ledgers from the opening sit on either side of the phase plane, the chain linking them through the diamond. On screen: 'per capita growth rate, per prey: r - aP', 'per capita growth rate, per predator: eaN - m'.
scenes.narration: So every kill, entered in both ledgers, ties them together. In this simple model, each population's per capita growth rate is set by the other's numbers.

scenes.visual: Hex end card. Take-home line: 'Each population's per capita growth rate is set by the other's numbers.'
